explanation: Cerebral cortical infarction typically causes upper motor neuron lesions resulting in spastic paralysis, as the corticospinal tract controls voluntary movement and its interruption leads to hypertonia and hyperreflexia.
Syringomyelia causes a characteristic 'cape' or 'jacket' distribution sensory loss due to the expansion of the syrinx affecting crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord.
Hemiballismus results from damage to the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, causing violent flinging movements of the opposite side of the body.
The corticostriatal pathway uses glutamate as its neurotransmitter, providing excitatory input from the cerebral cortex to the corpus striatum (caudate and putamen).
Static (resting) tremor in Parkinson's disease results from oscillatory activity between the globus pallidus interna and subthalamic nucleus due to loss of dopamine.
D1 receptors in the direct pathway are excitatory; dopamine binding to D1 receptors stimulates the direct pathway which ultimately facilitates movement via reduced GPi activity.
Corticostriatal fibers (cortex to corpus striatum) use glutamate as their neurotransmitter, providing the major excitatory input to the striatum.
The cerebellum corrects movements on the same side of the body through its deep cerebellar nuclei and their projections to the thalamus and motor cortex.

Climbing fibers originate from the inferior olivary nucleus, form powerful excitatory synapses on Purkinje cells, each Purkinje cell receives input from a single climbing fiber, and they play a role in motor learning.
Cerebellar lesions characteristically impair motor learning (adaptation of movements), as the cerebellum is essential for procedural memory and motor skill acquisition.
The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is responsible for the damping action that prevents overshoot and tremors during voluntary movements through its feedback loops.
The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) is primarily concerned with equilibrium and balance, receiving input from the vestibular apparatus.
Ipsilateral cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia due to loss of the cerebellum's facilitatory influence on alpha motor neurons and reduced gamma motor activity.
Intention tremor (present during voluntary movement, reduced during sleep) is characteristic of cerebellar dysfunction, as opposed to resting tremor seen in basal ganglia disorders.
Climbing fiber lesions specifically impair motor learning (adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex), as these fibers from the inferior olive encode error signals for cerebellar plasticity.
Neurons have reduced PFK-2/FBPase3 activity, resulting in low fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels, which inhibits glycolysis and makes neurons dependent on oxidative metabolism.
During excessive exercise, lactate produced by astrocytes serves as an energy source for neurons through the astrocyte-neuron lactate shuttle.
Ketone bodies are not a major energy source in the well-fed state; the brain preferentially uses glucose. They become important during starvation when glucose is scarce.
During starvation, the brain adapts to use ketone bodies (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate) as an alternative fuel when glucose availability decreases.
Neurons lack PFK2/FBPase3 (the bifunctional enzyme that produces fructose-2,6-bisphosphate), resulting in low glycolytic rate and dependence on oxidative metabolism.
5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid), the main metabolite of serotonin, is elevated in urine and used as a marker for carcinoid tumors that secrete serotonin.
Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors throughout the brain.
NADPH in astrocytes provides reducing equivalents for the glutathione reductase system, converting GSSG to reduced glutathione (GSH) to combat oxidative stress.
Pheochromocytoma (catecholamine-secreting tumor) causes elevated urinary VMA (vanillylmandelic acid), the main metabolite of epinephrine and norepinephrine.
Tryptophan is the precursor amino acid for serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) synthesis via the rate-limiting enzyme tryptophan hydroxylase.
Carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase, preventing conversion of levodopa to dopamine outside the CNS, allowing more levodopa to reach the brain.
GLUT1 is the glucose transporter predominantly expressed on astrocytes and the blood-brain barrier, facilitating glucose entry into the CNS.
Tyrosine hydroxylase (converting tyrosine to L-DOPA) is the rate-limiting step in catecholamine biosynthesis and requires tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor.
Urea is the final disposal form of amino groups in humans, produced in the liver through the urea cycle and excreted in urine.
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency prevents citrulline formation from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate; arginine becomes essential since the urea cycle cannot complete without it.
Urea contains two nitrogen atoms: one from ammonia (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from aspartate (via argininosuccinate synthetase reaction).
The branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine accumulate in maple syrup urine disease due to deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase.
Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, causing accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, and valine.

Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase; its deficiency impairs oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids.
PKU results from phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, causing accumulation of phenylalanine which is neurotoxic and leads to intellectual disability if untreated.
